summary:
Bangladesh's Penal Code of 1860 criminalises "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" under Section 377, punishable by imprisonment for life or by a term of up to ten years plus a fine. The explanation attached to the section treats penetration as sufficient and extends its ambit to any sexual union involving penile insertion, including consensual acts. Parliament declined to repeal the provision in 2009 and again in 2013. Prosecutions are rare, but police use the section to arrest, harass and extort people presumed to be LGBTIQ, and it has been invoked to restrict registration of LGBTI organisations. Whether the section reaches sex between women is unresolved: a UK Home Office country policy note updated in April 2026 records the ambiguity, noting that a 2019 ILGA report read female-female activity as not criminal while elsewhere describing the provision as relevant to all genders.

Enforcement operates through raid, extortion and public exposure rather than courtroom conviction. In a 2017 raid recorded in country human rights reporting, the paramilitary force RAB entered the Chayaneer Community Center in Keraniganj Upazila during an LGBTI dinner, separated the 120 people present into small groups, beat them and arrested 28 on suspicion of homosexual activity, allowed media to photograph some of those detained, and later stated the arrests were for narcotics possession. Four were remanded, twelve held for questioning and twelve sent directly to jail.

Visibly trans people, hijras in particular, face predatory policing. After hijras refused to pay police extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack in Gomdondi Phultala; on 17 September 2025 police in Narayanganj arrested twelve hijras for collecting money from expatriate-carrying vehicles, a traditional livelihood.

Transit points are not exempt. In April 2024 five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, according to the monitoring group JMBF.

Third-gender recognition exists on paper. On 11 November 2013 the cabinet chaired by Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina recognised hijras as a separate gender alongside male and female, and hijras hold legal third-gender status with gender-marker change permitted. Voter lists carry a third-gender option, and in April 2019 officials added "hijra" to voting forms. The recognition is narrow and unregulated: no policy sets out what a person must undergo to change gender on official documents, no criteria define who qualifies as a hijra, and no anti-discrimination protection covers hijras. Transgender communities other than hijras are neither recognised nor protected. A January 2015 Ministry of Health memorandum directed steps to identify hijras through medical check-ups requiring them to strip and have their genitals confirmed, with photographs later circulated to establish that hijras were "really men".

No form of relationship recognition exists. Bangladeshi law does not recognise same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships or adoption by same-sex couples, and same-sex couples have been detained and can be imprisoned or fined. A trans visitor in what would locally be classed as a same-sex relationship has no legal standing to protect a partner, and any couple read as same-sex under birth-sex status is exposed to detention.

The August 2024 ouster of Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina changed the security environment. A Washington Blade assessment published on 5 August 2025, a year after the protests, found LGBTQ people increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats. Hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground after the 2024 change, and trans people who had previously lived visibly were reported to be living in hiding.

Lethal violence against visible trans people continues. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district, on 3 February 2025; five unidentified individuals were accused and no outcome is documented.

JMBF's annual report, published in April 2026, documents 260 human rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across Bangladesh in 2025, described as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022. The conduct includes murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion. The figure is a raw count of documented cases without a population denominator, so it indicates the direction and scale of reporting rather than a per-capita risk rate.

Official statements reinforce the climate. Responding on 17 April 2022 to the U.S. Bangladesh 2021 Human Rights Report, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that treating LGBT rights and same-sex marriage as human rights was a regrettable and uncalled-for imposition of values by a select few countries. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019, in an asylum appeal by a Bangladeshi gay man, records Home Office country material describing Islamist groups calling for LGBT people to be prosecuted under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Institutional exclusion extends into education. In November 2023 transgender woman Hochemin Islam was excluded from the North South University women's carnival on security grounds amid student threats of unrest and an exam boycott. In August 2025 transgender woman Sahara Chowdhury, a final-year English student at Metropolitan University in Sylhet, was expelled for life on grounds she denied. In January 2024 a BRAC University lecturer publicly tore a seventh-grade textbook story about a hijra character, prompting student protests against LGBTQ content and a five-member Education Ministry review that four months later found nineteen words "incompatible" with Bangladeshi society and recommended their omission.
tangentialFactors:
The 2024 political transition removed a government that had refused to repeal Section 377 while extending third-gender recognition. The groups that gained ground afterwards campaign against LGBT visibility, and the effect on policing has been documented in the year that followed.

Advocacy and support infrastructure is thin. A 2017 U.S. Department of State report cited in country material records that after the Chayaneer raid and continued harassment many LGBTI organisation members, including leadership, reduced activities and sought refuge inside and outside the country, severely weakening networks; organisations specifically assisting lesbians are rare. A visitor relying on local NGOs for support should expect limited capacity.

Formal recognition and official practice diverge within the same system: the 2013 cabinet decision grants a document category, while the 2015 health ministry memorandum subjects applicants to genital inspection and public exposure. Neither is accompanied by anti-discrimination law.
localsOnly:
Hijras hold legal third-gender status, can change gender markers on official documents, appear on voter lists with a third-gender option and stand as candidates; a rural town elected a trans woman mayor in 2021.

State inclusion schemes exist alongside discrimination. A government housing scheme for homeless and landless people included transgender people for the first time, providing at least 140 government-built houses across the country. In December 2014 the Ministry of Social Welfare invited hijras to apply for government employment; in July 2015, after a hijra witnessed the murder of a secular blogger and helped arrest the perpetrators, the government announced plans to recruit hijras as traffic police. Bangladesh opened its first religious school for transgender people in Dhaka, with classes from 7 November 2020 for more than 150 expected students in Islamic and vocational subjects, free of charge and with no age limit.

Employment protections are narrow. Labour law prohibits wage discrimination on the basis of sex or disability but not other discrimination based on sex, disability, social status, caste, sexual orientation or similar factors, and no law protects against discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Health access is constrained by stigma. Country reporting notes that stigma against HIV and AIDS and against higher-risk populations is a barrier to health services, particularly for the transgender community and men who have sex with men. Hijras face severe discrimination and unequal access to housing and health care.
